title: Text Formatting & Inline Semantics
summary: Text elements show emphasis, importance, and other meaning.

subtopics.title: The document frame
subtopics.explanation: `<strong>` marks text with strong importance, seriousness, or urgency. Browsers often display it in bold, but the meaning is more than a visual weight. It is like emphasizing a warning in a spoken instruction. Use it for genuinely important words, not every phrase you want to look darker. For example, mark a safety warning as important, then use CSS to make it visually prominent. In a real page, use strong to mark an urgent instruction, not merely any bold label.

subtopics.title: Important pieces
subtopics.explanation: `<em>` marks stress emphasis that can change how a sentence is read. Browsers often display it in italics. It is like changing your voice to emphasize one word. Use it where the emphasis affects meaning, and use CSS when you only want an italic visual style. For example, emphasize a word when it changes how a sentence should be understood. In a real page, emphasis can change the stress in a sentence, not just its font style.

subtopics.title: Page information
subtopics.explanation: `<b>` and `<i>` can draw attention or mark alternate voice without adding strong importance or stress. Their exact use depends on the text. They are like a visual annotation rather than a warning. Prefer semantic elements when the meaning is important, and do not choose tags only for their default appearance. For example, use CSS italics for a title style when no alternate voice or semantic meaning is intended. In a real page, use code for a short property name that readers may copy.

subtopics.title: Content structure
subtopics.explanation: `<code>` marks a short fragment of computer code, such as a property name. It usually uses a monospace font. It is like switching to a typewriter face for a command. For multiple lines of code, place code inside `<pre>` so the spacing and line breaks are preserved. For example, wrap a short command in code, and use pre for a multi-line example. In a real page, place a block of code in pre so its spaces and line breaks remain.

subtopics.title: Good habits
subtopics.explanation: Choose HTML elements for meaning and use CSS for the visual design. This keeps the page understandable even when styles change or assistive technology reads it aloud. It is like writing clear stage directions before choosing costume colors. Check that emphasis remains understandable without relying on bold or italic alone. For example, check meaning with styles disabled so emphasis is not communicated by font shape alone. In a real page, use CSS for purely decorative italic text when it carries no semantic meaning.

foundations.overview: HTML text elements communicate what words mean, not only how they look. `<strong>` marks importance and `<em>` marks emphasis; CSS controls their visual appearance. Think of them like speaking cues in a script. Use semantic elements that match the message, then style them to fit the design. This helps browsers and assistive technology interpret the content consistently.
foundations.whyItMatters: Text semantics guide how content is announced and interpreted. Separating meaning from appearance keeps the message intact when styles, themes, or reading methods change.
commonUseCases: Display short and multi-line code examples.
Preserve meaning when CSS changes the visual style.
Show inline commands and multi-line code examples.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Bold text always means strong importance.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Visual weight and semantic importance are different; choose the element that matches the meaning.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A heading can be replaced with bold paragraph text.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Heading elements create a navigable document outline that bold styling does not provide.

commonMisconceptions.myth: CSS appearance determines what assistive technology announces.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Semantic HTML carries meaning independently of many visual style choices.

visualExplorer.title: Choosing semantic vs. presentational elements
visualExplorer.caption: Decide what a span of text means before styling it. These steps walk from intent to the right element.

config.intro: Two elements can look identical yet mean different things. Use this decision flow to pick the right one.

steps.name: Is it important or urgent?
steps.detail: If the text carries strong importance or seriousness (a warning, a key term), use <strong> — not just <b>.

steps.name: Does it stress meaning?
steps.detail: If emphasizing the word changes the sentence's meaning, use <em>. For an alternate voice (foreign phrase, term), use <i>.

steps.name: Is it code or a quote?
steps.detail: Inline code → <code>; a code block → <pre><code>; a long quote → <blockquote>; a short inline quote → <q>.

steps.name: Is it an abbreviation or formula?
steps.detail: Acronym → <abbr title="...">; subscript/superscript in a formula or footnote → <sub>/<sup>.

steps.name: Otherwise, just styling?
steps.detail: If you only want a visual effect with no meaning, use CSS — or <b>/<i>/<small> for purely stylistic offset.

interactiveExamples.title: Semantic emphasis and highlighting
interactiveExamples.explanation: Compare semantic <strong>/<em> against presentational <b>/<i>, and see <mark> and <small> in context. The defaults look familiar, but the meaning differs.

codeLab.instructions: This snippet uses <b>/<i> and a styling-only <span> where meaning exists. Replace them with the correct semantic elements: a warning's importance, true emphasis, inline code, and an abbreviation with its expansion.

keyTakeaways: `<strong>` marks text with strong importance, seriousness, or urgency.
`<em>` marks stress emphasis that can change how a sentence is read.
`<b>` and `<i>` can draw attention or mark alternate voice without adding strong importance or stress.
`<code>` marks a short fragment of computer code, such as a property name.
Choose HTML elements for meaning and use CSS for the visual design.
